analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agencies to address pollution burdens on communities of color and low-income communities, and tightens pollution permits.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 15 senators, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it law that every federal agency must identify and reduce pollution and health harms that fall disproportionately on communities of color, tribal communities, and low-income communities. It would have required air and water pollution permits to account for the combined pollution already in an area, and allowed permits to be denied or tightened when adding more pollution would put nearby residents' health at risk. It also would have created new ways for individuals to sue over discriminatory practices and pollution harms, and continued roughly $10 million a year in small grants to affected communities.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near polluting facilities — disproportionately low-income communities, communities of color, and tribal communities — would gain stronger health protections, better information about pollution in their neighborhoods, and new legal tools to challenge discriminatory or harmful pollution decisions. Community organizations could also apply for federal grants to address local environmental health problems.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal agency to make addressing disproportionate health and environmental harms to communities of color, indigenous communities, and low-income communities part of its mission, with annual strategies and public progress reports [S3].

Amends the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act so that permits for discharges and major air sources must account for cumulative pollution already affecting the area, and cannot be issued or renewed unless there is a reasonable certainty of no harm to nearby residents' health [S2].

Requires major air source applicants to analyze community demographics, nearby schools, day care centers, nursing homes, hospitals, and existing pollution before a permit is granted, and lets regulators deny permits to persistent violators [S3].

Creates a private right of action under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act for anyone aggrieved by discriminatory practices, and preserves implied rights of action and common law claims under major environmental laws [S2].
Continues EPA's environmental justice small grants, collaborative problem-solving agreements, and CARE grant programs, with $10 million authorized per year for fiscal years 2018 through 2027 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities that hold air and water pollution permits — such as chemical plants, power plants, and manufacturers — would bear new costs: cumulative impact analyses, additional controls or pollution prevention requirements, possible permit denials, and heightened legal exposure from new rights of action.

drawbacks.text: The bill's permitting standard — a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' before any permit is issued or renewed, judged against all cumulative pollution in the area — is far stricter than current law and could make routine permit renewals slower, costlier, and harder to obtain for many facilities [S3].

Broad new rights of action, including a private right of action under Title VI that applies to pending cases, would open the door to more litigation against regulated entities and entities receiving federal funds [S3].

The $10 million annual grant authorization is small relative to the scope of the mandate, and the bill's requirements for every federal agency would impose significant administrative workloads without dedicated funding beyond the grants [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities living near concentrated pollution, the bill offered concrete protections — cumulative impact review, permit denials for chronic violators, and standing to sue — that current law does not provide. The costs fall on permitted industrial facilities and would partly take the form of better analysis and pollution controls, which is the point of the bill; the strongest honest objection is that the strict 'no harm' standard and expanded litigation rights could slow legitimate permitting and generate legal disputes that are not always well-founded.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on October 24, 2017 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
Fifteen senators cosponsored the bill: 14 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — so it never received a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial permit holders and other regulated facilities are better off because the bill never advanced: the stricter cumulative-impact permitting standard, persistent-violator permit denials, and new litigation rights never took effect. Communities near pollution sources gained nothing.

for.name: Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 2017 in the Senate and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 14 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the only support it received in the chamber.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent, Bernie Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Industrial air and water permit holders (chemical plants, power plants, manufacturers)
industries.note: The bill would have required their permits to account for all pollution already in the surrounding area, allowed denials for persistent violators, and exposed them to new lawsuits. Its central mechanism is to reduce the pollution these facilities put into nearby communities.

Mandatory cumulative impact analyses for major air sources and permit renewals would create demand for the demographic, air quality, and public health studies the bill requires. Better analysis serves the communities the bill targets.
